name: Punjabi
variety: Standard Punjabi based on the Majhi dialect, as written in Gurmukhi (Indian Punjab). Tone numerals and formants come from the Lyallpuri (Faisalabad) variety of Hussain et al. 2020, tone acoustics also from Indian Punjabi speakers (Evans et al. 2018).
sources: Hussain, Qandeel; Proctor, Michael; Harvey, Mark & Demuth, Katherine (2020). Punjabi (Lyallpuri variety). Journal of the International Phonetic Association 50(2), 282-297.
Bhatia, Tej K. (1993). Punjabi: A Cognitive-Descriptive Grammar. London: Routledge.
Gill, Harjeet Singh & Gleason, Henry A. (1962). A Reference Grammar of Panjabi. Hartford: Hartford Seminary Foundation.
Shackle, Christopher (2003). Panjabi. In Cardona, George & Jain, Dhanesh (eds.), The Indo-Aryan Languages. London: Routledge.
Bailey, Thomas Grahame (1914). A Panjabi Phonetic Reader. London: University of London Press.
Bhatia, Tej K. (1975). The evolution of tones in Punjabi. Studies in the Linguistic Sciences 5(2), 12-24.
Bhardwaj, Mangat Rai (2016). Panjabi: A Comprehensive Grammar. London: Routledge.
Dhillon, Rajdip (2010). Stress and Tone in Indo-Aryan Languages. PhD dissertation, Yale University.
Bowden, Andrea L. (2012). Punjabi Tonemics and the Gurmukhi Script: A Preliminary Study. MA thesis, Brigham Young University.
Kanwal, Jasmeen & Ritchart, Amanda (2015). An experimental investigation of tonogenesis in Punjabi. Proceedings of the 18th International Congress of Phonetic Sciences, Glasgow.
Evans, Jonathan; Yeh, Wen-Chi & Kulkarni, Rukmini (2018). Acoustics of tone in Indian Punjabi. Transactions of the Philological Society 116(3), 509-528.
Hussain, Qandeel (2015). Temporal characteristics of Punjabi word-medial singletons and geminates. Journal of the Acoustical Society of America 138(4), EL388-EL392.

Hussain, Qandeel; Proctor, Michael; Harvey, Mark & Demuth, Katherine (2017). Acoustic characteristics of Punjabi retroflex and dental stops. Journal of the Acoustical Society of America 141(6), 4522-4542.
Masica, Colin P. (1991). The Indo-Aryan Languages. Cambridge University Press.

vowel_formants.speaker: adult male (one 30-year-old speaker of Lyallpuri Punjabi, word-medial vowels, mean of 5 tokens)
vowel_formants.notes: The source reports F1 and F2 only; the third value is null. The source writes the long vowels without a length mark.

contrasts: three-way laryngeal contrast in stops and affricates: voiceless unaspirated, voiceless aspirated, voiced. The breathy voiced series of the script (ਘ ਝ ਢ ਧ ਭ) no longer exists as such and is reflected in tone.
lexical tone on the stressed syllable: /kòːɽaː/ 'horse' (low), /koːɽaː/ 'whip' (mid), /kóːɽaː/ 'leper' (high)
dental versus retroflex stops; /n/ : /ɳ/; /l/ : /ɭ/; tap /ɾ/ versus retroflex flap /ɽ/
three short central vowels /ɪ ə ʊ/ against seven long peripheral vowels
oral versus nasal vowels for the seven peripheral vowels
consonant gemination for 19 consonants, always after a short central vowel (/pət̪aː/ 'address' : /pət̪ːaː/ 'leaf')
loan fricatives /f z x ɣ/ are used by educated and urban speakers only
allophony: palatal [ɲ] and velar [ŋ] nasals are allophones of /n/ before palatal and velar stops
/ɳ ɽ ɭ/ occur only word-medially and word-finally
/ɦ/ occurs word-initially; after a vowel it has been lost, leaving a high tone
retroflex stops have shorter closure and shorter release than dentals and pull F2 and F3 of the preceding vowel together (Hussain et al. 2017)
the rhotic is a tap; the retroflex flap lowers F3 and F4 early
historically breathy voiced stops are voiceless unaspirated word-initially and plain voiced elsewhere (Kanwal & Ritchart 2015)
tones are fully realised on stressed syllables; on unstressed syllables they shrink to a raised pitch or disappear (Evans et al. 2018)
syllable_structure: (C)V(V)(C)(C); no initial clusters in native words; final clusters are rare and mostly in loans; lexical words have at least two moras
phonotactics: geminates occur only after /ɪ ə ʊ/
word-final clusters are fricative or rhotic plus stop (/sʊst̪/ 'lazy', /mərd̪/ 'man')
inside roots a stop that follows a heterorganic nasal is always voiceless
central vowels do not contrast in nasality and do not end diphthongs

stress.rule: Light (short vowel, open), heavy (long vowel, or short vowel plus coda) and superheavy (long vowel plus coda) syllables: in disyllables the leftmost superheavy syllable is stressed, otherwise the penultimate; in trisyllables the penultimate or antepenultimate, never the final (Dhillon 2010; Hussain et al. 2020).
stress.cues: duration, with higher pitch and greater loudness reported impressionistically; tone is carried by the stressed syllable

rhythm.vowel_reduction: moderate: short vowels are centralised and unstressed syllables are shortened; no phonemic reduction of long vowels
rhythm.notes: Stress is more audible than in Hindi, but no rhythm metric could be verified; class and final lengthening are my assessment.

length.notes: Peripheral vowels are long (two moras), central vowels short (one mora). Geminate stops have a longer closure; their total duration is about 40 percent greater than that of singletons (Hussain 2015). Low-tone vowels are the longest and high-tone vowels the shortest.

intonation.declarative: toneless words follow the areal pattern, with pitch rising across the word or phrase and a final fall; tonal syllables impose their own contour on the stressed syllable
intonation.wh_question: prominence on the wh-word, final fall
intonation.continuation: rise at the end of non-final phrases
intonation.accent_shape: L* ... H on toneless phrases; on tonal words the lexical contour replaces the low start
intonation.notes: Kanwal & Ritchart 2015 observed a general rise on word-final syllables of toneless words, as in an accentual-phrase language. How the lexical tones combine with boundary tones has not been described.

inventory.name: low tone (grave accent; traditionally 'low' or 'low-rising')
inventory.description: Pitch starts high, falls steeply to the lowest target of the three tones and rises a little at the end. Arises on the stressed vowel that follows a historical breathy voiced stop: word-initially the stop is now voiceless unaspirated (ਘੋੜਾ /kòːɽaː/ 'horse', ਭਾਰ /pàːɾ/ 'weight'), before a stressed non-initial vowel it is plain voiced (ਸੁਧਾਰ /sʊd̪àːɾ/ 'reform').

inventory.name: mid tone (unmarked, neutral)
inventory.description: Level or slightly falling mid pitch in citation form; in phrases it takes the intonational contour. All syllables without a historical breathy stop or postvocalic h.

inventory.name: high tone (acute accent; traditionally 'high' or 'high-falling')
inventory.description: Pitch is raised at the end of the vowel; in longer words the peak comes late in the stressed syllable and the fall follows on the next syllable. Arises on the stressed vowel before a historical breathy voiced stop, which is now plain voiced (ਮਾਘ /máːɡ/, ਕੁਝ /kʊ́dʒ/ 'some'), and before a lost h (ਚਾਹ /tʃáː/ 'tea', ਬਾਹਰ /báːɾ/ 'outside'); the subscript h of the script marks it after sonorants (ਪੜ੍ਹ /pə́ɽ/ 'read', ਕੋੜ੍ਹਾ /kóːɽaː/ 'leper').

sandhi: no tone sandhi is described; a word has at most one tone, on its stressed syllable
on unstressed syllables the tone is reduced to a raised pitch without a fall, or is not realised (Evans et al. 2018)
tone.neutral_tone: Syllables without lexical tone are mid and follow the phrase intonation: pitch rises across the word, with the peak at the end of the phrase.
tone.notes: The Chao numerals are the ones printed in Hussain et al. 2020 (Figure 9) for one male speaker's citation forms /tʃáː/, /tʃaː/, /tʃàː/. Acoustic studies of Indian Punjabi agree on the low tone: after an initial historical breathy stop the pitch starts high and falls, from a maximum of 102-143 Hz to a minimum of 94-129 Hz in five male speakers (a fall of roughly 8 to 19 Hz), high-falling for most and mid-falling for some (Kanwal & Ritchart 2015; Evans et al. 2018), not the low-rising shape of the older descriptions (Gill & Gleason 1962; Bhatia 1993). Evans et al. treat the system as one privative falling tone whose position in the word differs. The tones arose when the breathy voiced stops and postvocalic h were lost; the script still writes both, so tone is predictable from spelling and stress.

phonation: no contrastive breathy voice: the breathy voiced stops have merged with the voiceless unaspirated stops word-initially and with the voiced stops elsewhere
traces of breathiness on low-tone vowels are reported by some authors
Pakistani varieties keep more murmur and realise tone less regularly (Evans et al. 2018)

problems: There is one tone phoneme, written + and commented 'high tone', defined as Tone(5, 30, envelope/p_512): pitch raised above the intonation line, falling from the top of that range to the bottom by mid-vowel and rising slightly. The shape is that of the low tone [513]; the name is wrong, and it prints as a plain '+' in phoneme and IPA output.

The tone is inserted only by the spelling rules for word-initial ਘ ਝ ਧ ਭ, which also turn the stop into k, c, t, p. For ਢ the rule before a vowel sign has no tone mark, so ਢੋਲ and ਢਿੱਡ come out as [ʈol], [ʈɪɖ] without tone.
The high tone is never marked. Postvocalic ਹ and the subscript h are pronounced as [h]: ਚਾਹ [cah], ਬਾਹਰ [bahəɾ], ਪੜ੍ਹ [pʌɽh], ਕੋੜ੍ਹਾ [koɽha], ਮੂੰਹ [mũh].

Non-initial ਘ ਝ ਢ ਧ ਭ are pronounced as Hindi breathy voiced stops with no tone: ਕੁਝ [kʊɟʰ], ਦੁੱਧ [dʊdʰ], ਮਾਘ [maɡʰ], ਸਿੰਘ [sɪ̃ɡʰ], ਸੁਧਾਰ [sʊdʰaɾ]. Punjabi has plain voiced stops there, with high tone before them or low tone after them.
Gemination written with addak is lost before a word-final consonant (ਸੱਚ [sʌc], ਹੱਥ [hʌtʰ], ਅੱਖ [ʌkʰ]) and for the five tone letters, which have no addak rules (ਦੁੱਧ, ਬੁੱਢਾ).
A vowel with tippi becomes a nasal vowel and the nasal consonant is dropped before a stop: ਅੰਬ [ʌ̃b], ਮੁੰਡਾ [mʊ̃ɖa] for [əmb], [mʊɳɖaː].
/ʋ/ is the fricative [v] of the base table; the retroflex flap has no IPA name and prints as 'r.'.
Intonation uses the generic eSpeak tunes and takes no account of the lexical tones.
good: word-initial ਘ ਝ ਧ ਭ are devoiced and deaspirated and the following vowel gets a falling-rising contour, which is what acoustic studies report for the low tone
short central and long peripheral vowels differ in quality and length
retroflex nasal, lateral and flap are present

notes: The Shahmukhi (Perso-Arabic) spelling used in Pakistan is not handled by this voice. The diphthong list is that of Hussain et al. 2020. /f z x ɣ/ are loan phonemes. No VOT table could be verified, so voice_onset_time_ms is left out.
